solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A lot of ice cream's melting in pots, perhaps

indicators.note: melting things lose their shape, so the letters are reformed in a new order
a lot of something is most but not all of it, so a letter is lost

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A tub of ice cream is going soft in its containers.
explanation.walkthrough: One of the three Es goes, then the remaining eight letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Pots are an example of fired clay ware, which is what ceramics are, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Current account opened by e.g. Queen of Hearts?

indicators.note: something opened by another thing has that other thing at its start

parts.note: a queen is an example of a playing card
I is the symbol for electric current
AC is short for account

explanation.surface: The Queen of Hearts from Alice opens a bank account.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Queen of Hearts' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'e.g. Queen' is wordplay and 'of Hearts' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cardiac is the adjective relating to the heart, so 'of hearts' describes it.

clue.text: Run champion dog here?

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run
an ace is a champion performer
to dog someone is to track them

explanation.surface: A place where a winning greyhound might race.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue doubles as the definition: a champion greyhound would run at such a venue.
explanation.definitionFit: A racetrack is the course where dogs or horses compete in races.

clue.text: Current supplier of publication, after tax, getting nothing

parts.note: mag is short for magazine
net pay is what remains after tax
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A modern magazine supplier earns nothing once tax is paid.
explanation.definitionFit: A magneto is a small generator, as in old engines, which supplies electric current.

clue.text: My second tune, one from The Pirates of Penzance?

definitions.text: one from The Pirates of Penzance?

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like 'my!'
S is the abbreviation for second
an air is a tune

explanation.surface: Someone humming their second favourite song from the Gilbert and Sullivan operetta.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pirates of Penzance is a Gilbert and Sullivan operetta; the question mark allows any pirate from it.
explanation.definitionFit: A corsair is a pirate, so one of the operetta's pirates would be a corsair.

clue.text: Poet curtailed attempt to install program

indicators.note: installing something puts it inside, so one piece goes within the other
curtailed means cut short at the tail, so the last letter goes

parts.note: a shot is an attempt
an app is a computer program

explanation.surface: A poet gives up partway through trying to set up some software.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curtailed' looks as if it describes the poet, but it applies to the attempt; a program from the modern sense of software is wedged inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Sappho was the ancient Greek lyric poet of Lesbos.

clue.text: Individual is to divulge info in two different ways

parts.note: first way: an informer sings to the police
second way: to let on is to reveal a secret

explanation.surface: A person sharing information through two separate routes.
explanation.walkthrough: One phrase supplies two synonyms: the setter asks for two different words both meaning to divulge.
explanation.definitionFit: A singleton is a single person or thing on its own, an individual.

clue.text: Napoleon, say, receiving message about old fashion item

indicators.note: receiving something takes it in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: Napoleon is the pig who rules in Orwell's Animal Farm

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: a wire is a telegram

explanation.surface: The French emperor gets a dispatch about an antique bit of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon looks like the emperor, but here he is Orwell's pig.
explanation.definitionFit: A periwig is a powdered wig of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, an outdated accessory.

clue.text: Prince Charlie with that old-fashioned calm

parts.note: Prince Hal is Shakespeare's young Henry V
Charlie is C in the NATO alphabet
yon is an archaic word for that

explanation.surface: Bonnie Prince Charlie keeping a quaint composure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince Charlie' reads as one name, but splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Halcyon means calm and peaceful, as in halcyon days.

clue.text: How to create danger in decorative outside area

parts.note: surface reading: a way of causing peril
setter's reading: shake up the letters of a word for a plot of land and you get the word danger

explanation.surface: Instructions for making something hazardous in a garden setting.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse anagram: ROCK is the instruction to stir and GARDEN is the fodder, whose letters rearranged spell DANGER.
explanation.definitionFit: A rock garden is an ornamental plot of stones and alpine plants laid out in a yard.

clue.text: Character shown by king given cry of encouragement

parts.note: R is short for rex, king
the Spanish cheer of the bullring

explanation.surface: A part in a play is given to a king with a cheer.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's role is the character played in a production.

clue.text: Obstructive about a film excited Yankee's expecting

indicators.note: about means going around, so one phrase surrounds the rest

parts.note: something obstructive is in the way

indicators.note: excited things are stirred up, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
Yankee is Y in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: An awkward American is getting worked up about a movie.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged A FILM plus Y makes FAMILY, which sits inside IN THE WAY; the 's is a contraction of 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the family way is an old-fashioned idiom for pregnant, as is expecting.

clue.text: Affair which follows case of criminal racket

indicators.note: following places one piece after another in sequence
a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters of the next word count

parts.note: first and last letters of the word
an amour is a love affair

explanation.surface: An affair comes after a court case involving a criminal.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket is a loud noise, and clamour is a synonym for a noisy din.

clue.text: Turned out coats the setter's put on market at first with no reductions

indicators.note: coating something covers it, so the scrambled word wraps around what follows
out here means disordered, so the preceding word's letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
the setter is I, and setter's is I'm

indicators.note: at first points to the opening letter only

parts.note: first letter of the word

explanation.surface: Coats I made turned out and went on sale without any discount.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' looks like one phrase meaning produced; 'Turned' is the fodder and 'out' scrambles it.
explanation.definitionFit: Untrimmed means not cut back, so nothing has been reduced.

clue.text: Putting on smart clothing heading for amateur golf

indicators.note: clothing something covers it, so one part wraps around others

parts.note: to smart is to sting

indicators.note: a heading is at the top, so just the first letter is wanted

parts.note: first letter of the word
Golf is G in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Getting dressed in stylish kit before a round of amateur golf.
explanation.definitionFit: Staging a play means mounting a production of it, as putting on a play does.

clue.text: Conclude Panama, say, is not productive

parts.note: to infer is to conclude
a Panama is a hat, and tile is slang for a hat

explanation.surface: Deciding that the Central American country is economically barren.
explanation.walkthrough: Panama looks like the country, but here it is the straw hat; tile is old slang for a hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Infertile means unable to produce crops or offspring, hence unproductive.

clue.text: German agreed to invest a thousand, with skill to make capital

indicators.note: to invest is to clothe or surround, so the first word encloses what follows

parts.note: ja is German for yes
taken as written
K stands for a thousand
art is skill, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: A German consents to put a large sum into an artistic enterprise to grow his capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Capital looks like money in this financial surface, but it is a capital city.
explanation.definitionFit: Jakarta is the capital city of Indonesia.

clue.text: Strauss heroine's death coming up after song

indicators.note: after places this piece following the other

parts.note: an aria is an operatic song

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means travelling upwards, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: death is the end

explanation.surface: The heroine of a Strauss opera dies after her big number.
explanation.definitionFit: Ariadne is the title heroine of Richard Strauss's opera Ariadne auf Naxos.

clue.text: Figure in performing arts taking pessimistic view

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so one word sits within the other
performing suggests putting on an act, so these letters are put through their paces in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
two is a figure, a number

explanation.surface: A personality in the performing arts with a gloomy outlook.
explanation.definitionFit: At worst introduces the most pessimistic outcome, as in 'at worst we'll lose'.

clue.text: Maybe people who like Tolkien books back in nick

indicators.note: going back means reading the letters from the end to the start

parts.words: Maybe people who like Tolkien books
parts.note: admirers of Tolkien might be called elf fans, 'maybe' flagging the loose definition

explanation.surface: Fans of Tolkien might be locked up in a prison cell with his books.
explanation.walkthrough: Nick is British slang both for prison and for steal; the definition is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To snaffle and to nick are both informal British words for stealing.

clue.text: Wise remark introducing philosopher's works

indicators.note: something introducing another comes first, before it

parts.note: a saw is an old saying
John Stuart Mill, the English philosopher

explanation.surface: A proverb opening a collection of a thinker's writings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Philosopher's works' looks like his books; the 's is 'is', and works means a factory.
explanation.definitionFit: Works can mean an industrial site, and a sawmill is a plant where timber is cut.

clue.text: A sailor heard being offensive

definitions.note: the noun sense: an offensive is an attack

indicators.note: heard tells us the sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: a salt is an old sailor

explanation.surface: A seaman was overheard being rude.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being offensive' reads as rude, but offensive here is the military noun, an attack.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault is an attack, and an offensive is an attacking campaign.

clue.text: Court toured by English count with upright bearing

parts.note: E is short for English

indicators.note: a place toured by someone is gone all round, so one piece is enclosed

parts.note: to count on is to rely on
CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: An English earl tours the royal court, holding himself straight.
explanation.walkthrough: Count looks like a nobleman, but it is the verb, as in count on.
explanation.definitionFit: Erectly means in an upright position, with bearing describing posture.

clue.text: Cherish new view set out in war story

indicators.note: setting things out arranges them afresh, so these letters take a new order

parts.note: the fourteen letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Treasure a fresh perspective laid out in a war narrative.
explanation.definitionFit: In Which We Serve is Noel Coward's 1942 naval war film, so it is a war story.

clue.text: Heading back, go for another look in river

indicators.note: heading back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: to redo is to go over again

explanation.surface: Turning round to have a second look at something in a river.
explanation.definitionFit: The Oder is a river of central Europe forming part of the German-Polish border.

clue.text: Frantic legal eagle judge dismissed, one doing filing?

parts.note: manic means frantic

indicators.note: someone dismissed is sent away, so that letter leaves the word

parts.note: a jurist is an expert in law
J is the abbreviation for judge

explanation.surface: A panicking lawyer sacked by a judge, perhaps a clerk doing the paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: The filing is of nails, not documents, as the question mark hints.
explanation.definitionFit: A manicurist trims and shapes nails with a file, so is literally someone doing filing.

clue.text: Teen cycling during a couple of days with depression

indicators.note: during means within a span of time, so one piece sits inside another
cycling moves a letter from one end round to the other

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for day, twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: A teenager riding a bike for two days ends up feeling low.
explanation.walkthrough: Cycling a word moves its first letter round to the end; 'depression' suggests low mood but means a dent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something dented has a hollow or dip pushed into it, which is a depression in its surface.

clue.text: Aboard jet, accessory maker wants hot flannel

indicators.note: aboard means on board inside a vessel, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: to jet somewhere is to fly

indicators.note: wants here means lacks, so that letter is missing

parts.note: a hatter makes hats, accessories
H is the abbreviation for hot, on taps

explanation.surface: On a plane, a fashion designer asks for a hot towel.
explanation.walkthrough: Flannel is British slang for smooth talk as well as a face cloth, which is what the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Flannel in British English means insincere smooth talk, which is flattery.
